solutions.title: Triangle inequality on each coordinate
solutions.body:
For $P=(x,y)$:
$$d_T(A,P)+d_T(P,B)=\big(|x|+|4-x|\big)+\big(|4-y|+|y|\big)\ge x+(4-x)+(4-y)+y=8=d_T(A,B),$$
using $|r|\ge r$, with equality iff $x\ge0$, $4-x\ge0$, $4-y\ge0$, $y\ge0$. So the set is the square $0\le x\le4$, $0\le y\le4$ (boundary included). ∎

solutions.title: Case analysis
solutions.body: Inside the square ($0\le x,y\le4$) the sum is $x+(4-y)+(4-x)+y=8$. If, say, $x<0$ and $0\le y\le4$, the sum is $(-x)+(4-y)+(4-x)+y=8-2x>8$; similarly for $x>4$, $y<0$, $y>4$ (each out-of-range coordinate adds twice its excess). So exactly the square works. ∎

**Answer: $(3,4)$**

solutions.body:
$\angle BOA=\angle AOP$ means ray $OB$ is the reflection of ray $OP$ across line $OA$ (direction $(2,1)/\sqrt5$). Reflecting $(1,0)$: $2\,\frac{(1,0)\cdot(2,1)}{5}(2,1)-(1,0)=\frac45(2,1)-(1,0)=\left(\frac35,\frac45\right)$. So $(m,n)=(3,4)$.

answer: $d_E(O,A)=d_T(O,A)$, and $d_T(O,B)=d_E(O,B)\,(|\cos\angle AOB|+|\sin\angle AOB|)$ by dropping the perpendicular from $B$ to line $OA$.

solutions.title: Drop a perpendicular
solutions.body:
Since $OA$ is horizontal, $d_E(O,A)=d_T(O,A)$, so $\cos_T\angle AOB=\dfrac{d_E(O,B)}{d_T(O,B)}\cos\angle AOB$.

$$\cos_T\angle AOB=\frac{\cos\angle AOB}{|\cos\angle AOB|+|\sin\angle AOB|}.\ ∎$$

*(Power Question 2016: Taxicab Geometry.)* For points $A=(x_1,y_1)$ and $B=(x_2,y_2)$, the Euclidean distance is $d_E(A,B)=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}$ and the **taxi-distance** is $d_T(A,B)=|x_2-x_1|+|y_2-y_1|$. The **taxi-cosine** and **taxi-sine** of an angle are
$$\cos_T\angle ACB=\frac{d_E(C,A)\,d_E(C,B)}{d_T(C,A)\,d_T(C,B)}\cos\angle ACB,\qquad \sin_T\angle ACB=\frac{d_E(C,A)\,d_E(C,B)}{d_T(C,A)\,d_T(C,B)}\sin\angle ACB,$$
where $\cos$ and $\sin$ are the ordinary (Euclidean) functions.

Let $\overrightarrow{QP}$ be parallel to the $x$-axis, and let $A$ and $B$ be points not on $\overrightarrow{QP}$. Show that
$$\cos_T\angle AQB=\frac{\cos\angle AQB}{\big(|\cos\angle AQP|+|\sin\angle AQP|\big)\big(|\cos\angle BQP|+|\sin\angle BQP|\big)}.$$
answer: For any point $X$, $d_T(Q,X)=d_E(Q,X)\,(|\cos\angle XQP|+|\sin\angle XQP|)$ since $QP$ is horizontal; substitute for $X=A,B$.

solutions.title: Taxi-length via the horizontal
solutions.body:
Let $A'$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to line $PQ$ (horizontal). Then $QA'$ is horizontal and $A'A$ vertical, so
$$d_T(Q,A)=d_E(Q,A')+d_E(A',A)=d_E(Q,A)\big(|\cos\angle AQP|+|\sin\angle AQP|\big).$$
Similarly $d_T(Q,B)=d_E(Q,B)\big(|\cos\angle BQP|+|\sin\angle BQP|\big)$. Substituting these into
$\cos_T\angle AQB=\dfrac{d_E(Q,A)d_E(Q,B)}{d_T(Q,A)d_T(Q,B)}\cos\angle AQB$ gives the formula. ∎

*(Power Question 2016: Taxicab Geometry.)* For points $A=(x_1,y_1)$ and $B=(x_2,y_2)$, the Euclidean distance is $d_E(A,B)=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}$ and the **taxi-distance** is $d_T(A,B)=|x_2-x_1|+|y_2-y_1|$. The **taxi-cosine** and **taxi-sine** of an angle are
$$\cos_T\angle ACB=\frac{d_E(C,A)\,d_E(C,B)}{d_T(C,A)\,d_T(C,B)}\cos\angle ACB,\qquad \sin_T\angle ACB=\frac{d_E(C,A)\,d_E(C,B)}{d_T(C,A)\,d_T(C,B)}\sin\angle ACB,$$
where $\cos$ and $\sin$ are the ordinary (Euclidean) functions. Triangle $ABC$ has $\overline{AB}$ parallel to the $x$-axis, and the perpendicular dropped from $C$ to $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ meets $\overline{AB}$ at $C'$ and has taxi-length $h_T$. Let $a_T=d_T(B,C)$, $b_T=d_T(A,C)$, $c_T=d_T(A,B)$.

Prove that $a_T=b_T+c_T-2b_T\cos_T A$.

solutions.title: Decompose into horizontal and vertical legs
solutions.body:
Let $p=d_T(A,C')=d_E(A,C')$ and $q=d_T(B,C')=d_E(B,C')$ (horizontal segments), so $c_T=p+q$, $b_T=p+h_T$, $a_T=q+h_T$ (each of $AC$, $BC$ splits into a horizontal and a vertical leg). With Euclidean lengths $b=d_E(A,C)$, $a=d_E(B,C)$, $c=d_E(A,B)=c_T$, we have $p=b\cos A$, $q=a\cos B$, $h_T=b\sin A=a\sin B$.

By definition, $b_T\cos_TA=b_T\cdot\dfrac{b\,c}{b_T\,c_T}\cos A=b\cos A=p$ (using $c=c_T$). Therefore
$$b_T+c_T-2b_T\cos_TA=(p+h_T)+(p+q)-2p=q+h_T=a_T.\ ∎$$

solutions.body:
Let $p=d_T(A,C')=d_E(A,C')$ and $q=d_T(B,C')=d_E(B,C')$ (horizontal segments), so $c_T=p+q$, $b_T=p+h_T$, $a_T=q+h_T$ (each of $AC$, $BC$ splits into a horizontal and a vertical leg). *(Power Question 2016: Taxicab Geometry.)* For points $A=(x_1,y_1)$ and $B=(x_2,y_2)$, the Euclidean distance is $d_E(A,B)=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}$ and the **taxi-distance** is $d_T(A,B)=|x_2-x_1|+|y_2-y_1|$. The **taxi-cosine** and **taxi-sine** of an angle are
$$\cos_T\angle ACB=\frac{d_E(C,A)\,d_E(C,B)}{d_T(C,A)\,d_T(C,B)}\cos\angle ACB,\qquad \sin_T\angle ACB=\frac{d_E(C,A)\,d_E(C,B)}{d_T(C,A)\,d_T(C,B)}\sin\angle ACB,$$
where $\cos$ and $\sin$ are the ordinary (Euclidean) functions. Triangle $ABC$ has $\overline{AB}$ parallel to the $x$-axis, and the perpendicular dropped from $C$ to $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ meets $\overline{AB}$ at $C'$ and has taxi-length $h_T$. Let $a_T=d_T(B,C)$, $b_T=d_T(A,C)$, $c_T=d_T(A,B)$.

Prove that $c_T=\dfrac{a_T^2+b_T^2-2a_Tb_T\cos_T C}{a_T+b_T}$.

solutions.title: Use cos C = −cos(A+B)
solutions.body:
Let $p=d_T(A,C')=d_E(A,C')$ and $q=d_T(B,C')=d_E(B,C')$ (horizontal segments), so $c_T=p+q$, $b_T=p+h_T$, $a_T=q+h_T$ (each of $AC$, $BC$ splits into a horizontal and a vertical leg). With Euclidean lengths $b=d_E(A,C)$, $a=d_E(B,C)$, $c=d_E(A,B)=c_T$, we have $p=b\cos A$, $q=a\cos B$, $h_T=b\sin A=a\sin B$.

Since $C=\pi-A-B$, $\cos C=\sin A\sin B-\cos A\cos B$. Then
$$a_Tb_T\cos_TC=ab\cos C=(b\sin A)(a\sin B)-(b\cos A)(a\cos B)=h_T^2-pq.$$
With $p=b_T-h_T$ and $q=a_T-h_T$: $h_T^2-pq=h_T^2-(b_T-h_T)(a_T-h_T)=(a_T+b_T)h_T-a_Tb_T$. Hence
$$a_T^2+b_T^2-2a_Tb_T\cos_TC=a_T^2+b_T^2+2a_Tb_T-2(a_T+b_T)h_T=(a_T+b_T)(a_T+b_T-2h_T).$$
Finally $a_T+b_T-2h_T=p+q=c_T$, so dividing by $a_T+b_T$ gives the result. ∎

prompt:
*(Power Question 2016: Taxicab Geometry.)* For points $A=(x_1,y_1)$ and $B=(x_2,y_2)$, the Euclidean distance is $d_E(A,B)=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}$ and the **taxi-distance** is $d_T(A,B)=|x_2-x_1|+|y_2-y_1|$. The **taxi-cosine** and **taxi-sine** of an angle are
$$\cos_T\angle ACB=\frac{d_E(C,A)\,d_E(C,B)}{d_T(C,A)\,d_T(C,B)}\cos\angle ACB,\qquad \sin_T\angle ACB=\frac{d_E(C,A)\,d_E(C,B)}{d_T(C,A)\,d_T(C,B)}\sin\angle ACB,$$
where $\cos$ and $\sin$ are the ordinary (Euclidean) functions.

Given $\triangle ABC$, with $a_T=d_T(B,C)$, $b_T=d_T(A,C)$, $c_T=d_T(A,B)$, prove that $\dfrac{a_T}{\sin_T A}=\dfrac{b_T}{\sin_T B}=\dfrac{c_T}{\sin_T C}$.
answer: $\dfrac{c_T}{\sin_TC}=\dfrac{a_Tb_Tc_T}{abc}\cdot\dfrac{c}{\sin C}$, and similarly for the others; apply the Euclidean Law of Sines.

solutions.title: Reduce to the Euclidean Law of Sines
solutions.body:
Let $a,b,c$ be the Euclidean side lengths. By definition $\sin_TC=\dfrac{ab}{a_Tb_T}\sin C$, so
$$\frac{c_T}{\sin_TC}=\frac{a_Tb_Tc_T}{abc}\cdot\frac{c}{\sin C}.$$
Likewise $\dfrac{a_T}{\sin_TA}=\dfrac{a_Tb_Tc_T}{abc}\cdot\dfrac{a}{\sin A}$ and $\dfrac{b_T}{\sin_TB}=\dfrac{a_Tb_Tc_T}{abc}\cdot\dfrac{b}{\sin B}$. By the Euclidean Law of Sines $\frac a{\sin A}=\frac b{\sin B}=\frac c{\sin C}$, so the three taxi ratios are equal. ∎

solutions.title: Area
solutions.body:
From the definition, $d_T(C,A)\,d_T(C,B)\sin_T\angle ACB=d_E(C,A)\,d_E(C,B)\sin\angle ACB=2[ABC]$. Applying this at each vertex:
$$b_Tc_T\sin_TA=a_Tc_T\sin_TB=a_Tb_T\sin_TC=2[ABC].$$
Dividing by $a_Tb_Tc_T$ and taking reciprocals gives $\frac{a_T}{\sin_TA}=\frac{b_T}{\sin_TB}=\frac{c_T}{\sin_TC}$. ∎
